title: Quiz: Search Strategies and Numerical Optimisation

questions.text: Why does grid search become impractical when the number of model parameters is large?
options: Grid search only works for linear models
The number of grid points grows exponentially with the number of parameters
Grid search cannot compute RMSE for more than two parameters
optim() is always faster than grid search regardless of dimensionality
questions.explanation: With p parameters and n grid points per parameter, you need n^p evaluations. For p=10 and n=10, that is 10 billion evaluations — the curse of dimensionality.

questions.text: In optim(par = c(0, 0), fn = measure_distance, data = sim1), what does par = c(0, 0) specify?
options: The known true parameters of the model
The starting values from which the optimiser begins its search
The upper and lower bounds on the parameters
questions.explanation: par gives the starting point for the iterative optimiser. It does not know the true parameters — it searches from this point toward the minimum of the loss function.

questions.text: For RMSE on a standard linear model, optim() is guaranteed to find the global minimum regardless of starting values.
questions.explanation: RMSE for a linear model is a convex function — it has a single global minimum with no local minima. So any starting point will converge to the same optimal parameters (though speed may vary).

questions.text: In the RMSE landscape plot (a1 vs a2 coloured by RMSE), the low-RMSE region appears as:
options: A scattered cloud of random points
A circular blob in the centre of the plot
A narrow diagonal valley where both a1 and a2 are near their optimal values
An evenly distributed gradient across the entire parameter space
questions.explanation: The optimal (intercept, slope) pair lies at the bottom of a narrow elongated valley in the RMSE surface. This reflects the fact that many (a1, a2) pairs that deviate in opposite directions can partially compensate each other.

questions.text: purrr::map2_dbl(a1, a2, sim1_dist) applies sim1_dist to each pair of values in a1 and a2. What would happen if you used map_dbl(a1, sim1_dist) instead?
options: It would work identically, since map_dbl handles two arguments
It would fail because sim1_dist requires two arguments (a1 and a2)
It would use a2 = 0 for all calculations
It would return the RMSE for the full grid search instead
questions.explanation: map_dbl iterates over a single vector. sim1_dist(a1, a2) needs both arguments, so map2_dbl is required to iterate over both a1 and a2 in parallel.
